text:
Mutation testing offers a useful calibration principle: inject known faults, then measure whether diagnostics detect them. [DeepMutation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.05206) applies this idea to deep learning; [recommender metamorphic testing](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2024.107410) demonstrates checks based on relationships between executions when exact recommendation outputs lack an oracle. These support a calibration suite, but do not establish component-specific diagnostic accuracy for SASRec.

Proposed suite: evaluate bounded model copies with one mutation each—selected embedding-row corruption, disabled positional embeddings, broken causal masking, or candidate-score misalignment—alongside intact copies and restored copies. Measure detection rate by fault family, false alarms on intact/restored controls, and a fault-versus-probe confusion matrix. Verify each mutation actually changes its intended computation. SASRec’s tied input/output embeddings complicate attribution: embedding corruption can affect both history encoding and candidate scoring. Positional removal also need not reduce recommendation accuracy; the [original SASRec paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781) reports dataset-dependent ablation effects. Test causal masking by changing suffix tokens and checking earlier-position representations; final-position scores alone can miss future-information leakage. Candidate permutation should produce the corresponding score permutation in deterministic evaluation.

First enforce coverage prerequisites: all four dataset routes resolve, five real training users per category exist, histories contain valid local item IDs, and all 20 users receive full-catalog unseen-item recommendations. Missing panels mean diagnosis was not executed, rather than evidence of history insensitivity. Report coverage and explicit failure reasons before interpreting probe results. These implementation checks are proposed adaptations to the supplied task, not verified findings about the current run.
